about: Sections of an essay on romance by Joel (first person). In each, the sentences listed under "changed" were just rewritten; the rest is the essay as it stands. Read each section as it stands, with its heading.

texts.heading: Should you be in a relationship at all?
changed: People trigger each other and learn lessons, and sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.
Whether you should be in one depends on what you and the other person are ready for and have the resources for.
sentences: This is a horrible catch-22.
Wounded people get lonely, and loneliness itself can kill.
But the wounds that make somebody desperate for a relationship may also make them a terrible person to be in one with.
People trigger each other and learn lessons, and sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.
I’m pretty conservative about this, so I would tell most of my friends not to date yet.
First love your inner child.
If you can’t even do that, forget a relationship for now.
Get a cat or a puppy.
If you’re dishonest, can’t care what happens to another person, or keep turning every relationship into the same disaster, come on, you’re not ready.

You don’t have to be completely healed, but the present-day adult has to be able to parent whatever intimacy wakes up inside you, and responsible enough to deal with an actual child if sex creates one.
If you can’t be a parent in either sense, you aren’t ready to date.
A good relationship can teach you self-love too, which is part of the problem: you may need one most when you’re least capable of creating a good one, recognizing one, or keeping it good.
Whether you should be in one depends on what you and the other person are ready for and have the resources for.
Here’s a video that can help understand the long process.

texts.heading: Things get tricky fast
changed: An obvious problem dissolves into, “but I love her,” and right when both people most need a view from outside, the small world of the relationship starts feeling more real than the rest of life.
sentences: Couples withdraw from friends who aren’t supportive of the romantic dyad, and they also stop telling friends the whole truth.
Sharp questions start to feel rude.
An obvious problem dissolves into, “but I love her,” and right when both people most need a view from outside, the small world of the relationship starts feeling more real than the rest of life.
Sometimes withdrawing isn’t wrong: telling your friend, “Can you believe what my girlfriend is doing to me?” can be a privacy violation.
It’s just important to realize what is happening.

It doesn’t help if she tells her friends her side while I tell mine mine, so we need people who actually know both of us over time, well enough that the relationship isn’t the only reality in the room.
I’ll come back to that.

texts.heading: Don’t make your partner your whole world
changed: Part of why that little paradise feels like a magical wonderland is that you can suddenly stop parenting yourself now that you have someone who’s fully got your back.
sentences: When I’m in love, my partner is my everything.
Everything else drops away.
I still try to make some time for friends, but really all I want to do is be with her.
Part of why that little paradise feels like a magical wonderland is that you can suddenly stop parenting yourself now that you have someone who’s fully got your back.
This makes you soft and weak, kinda like a sweet treat or heroin.

It is wonderful to have their love and support, but don’t let that bring you away from your own self-love, reparenting, meditation, yoga, and other healing practices that keep you independently healthy.
Otherwise, you’ll end up blaming them when you feel bad.
So don’t let your world get so small.
Don’t abandon your friends unless they really aren’t good for the relationship.
And if they aren’t, ask why.
Are they bad friends?
Are they slyly interested in one of you romantically?
Or is the relationship so weak that it can’t handle anybody with an outside view?
You don’t need to spend as much time with friends as you did before the romance.
But keep some room to explore life on your own.

texts.heading: Different levels in different domains can be complementary
changed: They could pull me into life more, show me where I wasn’t seeing people, and sometimes be the skeptic when I was seeing the best in someone and missing their hidden motives.
sentences: I could teach these women about loving and reparenting their inner child, Buddhism, meditation, and other things I understood better.
They could pull me into life more, show me where I wasn’t seeing people, and sometimes be the skeptic when I was seeing the best in someone and missing their hidden motives.
When it works, we take turns, me teaching one day and learning the next, and that’s healthy.
It’s time to bring in other support once a partner has become the default caregiver and that’s taken for granted, or the romance could collapse under the burden.
Maybe the romance actually does need less intensity, maybe it becomes friendship, or maybe it ends.
Asking that question out loud is the first step in figuring it out, but I can’t answer it for others, and couldn’t always answer it for myself.
The next two sections are about masculine–feminine polarity and Twin Flames.
If neither is relevant to you, skip ahead to Two Pillars Don’t Hold The Roof Up.

texts.heading: Gaslighting in the dark
changed: But ask those friends for help fairly, with the goal of resolving the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation.
sentences: Do you have irreconcilable memories of key events?
I did with both my first and second wives.
I took my first wife, Ann, to two counselors.
The male counselor eventually told us, “I’ve never told anyone this, but you guys need to split up for at least six months.”

There’s no way to resolve a situation where one person remembers that you ruined her life on purpose, while you remember that she was having a manic episode and had to be committed for her own safety.
We also didn’t have mutual friends who could corroborate what happened—only friends on each side who were partial.
Many say it’s best to save face and work things out privately, but I’d disagree.
If you don’t have friends who can help with the conflict, then you’re really stuck (and you might wanna find some new friends).
But ask those friends for help fairly, with the goal of resolving the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation.
Both people should get a chance to speak, and good friends should hear both sides before validating either.
I can believe a friend’s experience and still tell them that my ability to know what is really going on is extremely limited.
If someone says, “I don’t have all the evidence,” I trust their thinking more.
Living in community would help because your friends would not only hear two stories afterward.
Sometimes they would actually see how the two of you treat each other when you argue.
If you’ve been there for someone, don’t abandon them in a crisis unless it’s unsafe for you to stay or they’re creating the crisis to keep you, or they aren’t willing to help themself.
You may need to arrange other care, but that’s no reason to pretend the romance still has a future.
